743.title: Draupadi's swayamvara
743.hook: a brahmin rises from the crowd and walks toward the bow
743.carry: the mark falls to the ground
743.howItsDone: Walking around something sacred to honor it, pradakshina, is part of Hindu worship: people walk around temple shrines, sacred trees and the wedding fire, keeping them on their right.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Karna at the bow, one sentence from the princess, and a glance at the sun. Your line was a glance at the sun.

The kings have failed. Karna has put down the bow. The arena goes quiet. From the benches where the brahmins sit, a young man stands up, dressed like any brahmin student. The brahmins around him murmur. Some are alarmed: where famous kings have failed, what's a brahmin going to do, except make the rest of us look foolish? Others look at his arms and the way he carries himself, and say: let him go.
screen: `THE ARENA GOES QUIET.` → `A BRAHMIN STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: It's Arjuna, in disguise. He walks up to the bow and around it, the text says, bows his head to Shiva, the giver of boons, and remembers Krishna. Then he picks it up. In a moment the bow is strung. He fits the arrows, shoots, and the mark falls to the ground, struck through the opening. The arena erupts. Flowers fall from the sky, the text says. There's music. Brahmins wave their cloths in the air. And Draupadi comes toward him and places her garland on him. Now keep the disguise in view. Arjuna is supposed to be dead. He's just won, in front of all the gathered kings, as a brahmin with no name. That's what makes the kings furious. A brahmin has taken the prize, they say, and they rise to fight. Bhima tears a tree out of the ground, strips it, and stands beside his brother holding it like a club. Between them, they hold the kings off. What's striking is the order of things. Before Arjuna lifts the bow, he walks around it, and bows. The strength comes after the bowing. And the man the arena can't name is the very one Drupada had the bow made for.
screen: `HE WALKS AROUND THE BOW AND BOWS.` · `THE MARK FALLS.` · `DRAUPADI'S GARLAND.` · `THE KINGS RISE; BHIMA TAKES A TREE.`

744.title: Draupadi's swayamvara
744.hook: two brothers come home with a princess, and their mother answers without looking
744.howItsDone: Bhiksha, food given as alms, is part of Hindu religious life: renunciants, and in some traditions students, receive food from householders, which is why the brothers, dressed as brahmins, call what they bring home alms.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the disguised archer bowed, strung the bow, and the mark fell. Your line was the mark falls to the ground.

Someone in the crowd has worked it out. While the kings fight, Krishna watches the brahmin with the bow and the giant with the tree, and turns to his brother Balarama. That one with the tree, he says, is Bhima. The archer is Arjuna. They didn't die in the fire. Meanwhile, at the potter's house where the family is staying, Kunti waits. It's late, and her sons haven't come back.

Bhima and Arjuna come to the door with Draupadi. They're living as brahmins, on alms, so they call in: look, we've brought alms. And Kunti, inside, without looking up, answers the way a mother might: share it, all of you. Then she sees who's standing there. A princess, not a bowl of rice. What have I said, Kunti cries, the text says. She can't simply take back her word, and she won't let it be false. So she takes Draupadi by the hand, goes to Yudhishthira, and asks how her word can stay true without wrong being done to the princess. Yudhishthira turns first to Arjuna: you won her, she's yours. Arjuna won't hear of it; the eldest should marry first. Then Yudhishthira sees all his brothers looking at Draupadi. He remembers words Vyasa once spoke, and fears the brothers could be divided over her if only one marries her. So he says she'll be the wife of all. A word said without looking. It happens in families: the yes called from the other room. What stands out isn't the slip. It's that Kunti treats her own word as weighty enough to need care, even when she didn't mean it. And then Krishna arrives at the potter's door with Balarama, and bows at Yudhishthira's feet. The cousins meet face to face.

745.title: Draupadi's swayamvara
745.hook: a king objects, and a sage tells him a story from another life
745.howItsDone: Draupadi's marriage is discussed in Hindu teaching and retelling; some retellings lean on Vyasa's account of her past life, and some modern novels tell the whole Mahabharata from Draupadi's side.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi's swayamvara came home: alms at the door, a mother's word given without looking, and Krishna arriving.

Drupada has a problem. His daughter was won by a brahmin no one could name, and now he learns who the man really is: Arjuna, alive, the one he'd hoped for from the start. Good news. Then Yudhishthira tells him the rest. Draupadi will be the wife of all five brothers. Drupada objects at once. One woman with many husbands, he says, is not the way of the Vedas or of custom. How can you, who know what's right, propose this?

Yudhishthira answers carefully. Dharma is subtle, he says, and its path is hard to see. He follows where those before him walked, and his mother has spoken. Then Vyasa arrives, and Drupada asks him directly: is this right, or not? Vyasa takes Drupada aside, alone, and tells him a story. In an earlier life, your daughter was a sage's daughter who couldn't find a husband. She practiced hard austerities, and Shiva came to grant her a wish. Give me a husband, she asked, again and again. And Shiva told her: since you asked more than once, in another birth you'll have more than one husband. Vyasa tells a second story too, of the five brothers as gods born on earth, and gives Drupada a sight beyond the ordinary, so he sees them shining as they truly are. Drupada is persuaded, and the weddings go ahead. Readers of the Mahabharata have argued over this, and the poem itself seems to know it. Count the reasons it gives: a mother's word, a brother's fear of division, a past life, a divine birth. Four answers to one question. Vyasa's stories carry the weight beyond the human world, and Drupada accepts them. And through all of it, look for Draupadi herself. In this whole scene she has almost nothing to say. Her voice comes later in the poem.
screen: `DHARMA IS SUBTLE.` · `VYASA'S STORY OF ANOTHER LIFE.` · `A WISH ASKED AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `SEVERAL REASONS, AND ONE SILENCE.`

746.title: Sabha: Indraprastha
746.hook: a burning forest, a builder spared, and the promise of a hall
746.howItsDone: Hindu tradition places the Pandavas' city of Indraprastha near present-day Delhi, and the name is still used for places there today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi's swayamvara ended in a wedding, after Drupada's objection and Vyasa's story. Your line was several reasons, and one silence.

A forest is on fire, and a man runs out of it. He's Maya, an asura and a master builder, with the flames at his back. Krishna, guarding the burning, raises his discus. Maya cries out to Arjuna to save him, and Arjuna answers: don't be afraid. A new book of the Mahabharata opens here, the Sabha Parva, the book of the hall, and it begins with a life spared, and a debt.
screen: `A FOREST ON FIRE.` → `MAYA CRIES OUT.` → `DON'T BE AFRAID.`

segments.voice: First, how the family got here. After the wedding, the Pandavas go back to Hastinapura, alive. Dhritarashtra gives them half the kingdom. Their half is Khandavaprastha, wild land, and there they build a city and call it Indraprastha. Then comes the burning of the Khandava forest, and Maya running out of it. Now, safe, Maya stands before Arjuna: you've saved me. Tell me what I can do for you. Arjuna won't take anything, the text says. In paraphrase: you've done enough; go, and be a friend to me. But Maya presses. He wants to give something. So Arjuna turns it over to Krishna, and Krishna asks for something that isn't for himself. Build a hall, he tells Maya, for Yudhishthira, so fine that no one who studies it could copy it. Here's the word for this new stretch: sabha. It means a hall, and also the assembly that meets in one. Notice how this hall begins. Not with a conquest, but with a life spared in a fire, and a debt the one who's owed doesn't want repaid. Arjuna refuses a reward. Krishna passes it on to the brother who'll sit in that hall as king. A gift handed along twice before a single stone is laid. Today, it's still a promise.
screen: `A CITY BUILT ON WILD LAND.` · `ARJUNA WON'T TAKE A REWARD.` · `KRISHNA ASKS FOR A HALL.` · then, large: `A GIFT HANDED ALONG TWICE.`

747.title: Sabha: Indraprastha
747.hook: Maya goes north for his materials, comes back with a mace and a conch, and builds a hall with a pool that looks like floor
747.carry: a hall opened by feeding a crowd
747.howItsDone: Moving into a new home, Hindu families often hold a griha pravesha, a house-entering ceremony, with a puja and a meal shared with guests before the family settles in.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a sabha promised to Yudhishthira by a builder who owed his life. Your line was a gift handed along twice.

Before Maya lays a single stone, he leaves. He goes north, past Kailasa, the text says, to a lake called Bindu, where he'd stored treasures long before. He comes back carrying gifts: a heavy mace bound in gold for Bhima, a conch called Devadatta, with a sound that carries, for Arjuna, and crystal and jewels and everything a hall like no other would need. Only then does he start building.
screen: `NORTH, PAST KAILASA.` → `A MACE FOR BHIMA.` → `A CONCH FOR ARJUNA.`

segments.voice: The text spends a long time on this hall. Walls that shine like the sun. Trees in bloom inside, and a cool breeze. In the middle, a pool: lotuses on the water, fish moving under them, crystal steps going down. The water was so still and clear that kings who came to see it, the text says, took it for solid floor, and fell in. Hold onto that pool; this serial will come back to it. Rakshasas called Kinkaras stood guard over the whole hall. Now watch what Yudhishthira does before he steps inside. He feeds a great crowd of brahmanas: rice and ghee, honey, fruit, meat for those who ate it. He gives away cows. There's music, there are offerings, and only after all that does he enter. A new place, opened by feeding people and giving things away. Then the hall fills. Sages come and sit in it. Kings come. Singers and musicians come. That's the second thing the word sabha holds. In Sanskrit it's a hall, and also the gathering that meets in it, the assembly. A sabha with no one in it is only a building. And at the heart of this one is a pool built to fool the eye. What looks like floor isn't. The Mahabharata doesn't say yet what that will cost. It lets the water sit there, clear and still, waiting.

748.title: Sabha: Indraprastha
748.hook: Narada walks into the new hall and, instead of praising it, starts asking the king questions
748.carry: each question opening with I hope
748.howItsDone: Narada's questions are read in Hindu tradition as a lesson in how to rule well, and they're often retold alongside the Mahabharata's other teachings on a king's duty, or rajadharma.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sabha opened by feeding a crowd, with a pool so clear that kings fell in. Your line was a hall opened by feeding a crowd.

A visitor walks into the new hall at Indraprastha and doesn't say a word about the building. Yudhishthira sits with his brothers, sages and kings around him. Then Narada comes in, the wandering sage, with other rishis behind him. The Pandavas stand, bow, and give him a seat. And Narada, looking at the king who owns this wonder, begins to ask him questions. Not about the crystal. About the kingdom.
screen: `NARADA ARRIVES.` → `A SEAT FOR THE SAGE.` → `QUESTIONS, NOT PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Narada's questions run on and on, and in the Sanskrit they lean on a small word, kaccit. It asks while hoping the answer is yes, something like: I hope that you are. A few, in paraphrase. Do you divide your time well between what's right, what's useful, and what's enjoyable? Are your ministers honest, and do they keep your counsel? Do your soldiers get their pay and food on time? Do you look after the families of men who died serving you? Do farmers have seed and food when they need it, and are there tanks and lakes across the land, so farming doesn't hang on the rain alone? Notice where these go. The hall is right there, shining. Narada's eyes go past it, to a soldier's widow, a farmer waiting for rain, a minister who might talk. A sabha is where a king sits to hear his people, and the sage is asking whether this one does. And the tone: kaccit doesn't accuse. It says, I hope this is so, and leaves room for the king to answer, and to fix what isn't so yet. Yudhishthira bows and says he'll do what's been asked, and the text has him glad to hear it. The first serious conversation in the new hall is a check-up on how the kingdom is run. The building is the occasion. The people are the point.
screen: `KACCIT: I HOPE THAT YOU ARE.` · `SOLDIERS, WIDOWS, FARMERS.` · `PAST THE HALL, TO THE PEOPLE.` · `ASKED IN HOPE, NOT ACCUSATION.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE ARE THE POINT.`

segments.voice: Choose one part of your life that other people depend on: a household, a team, a friendship, a job. Ask it one question the way Narada asks, beginning with I hope: I hope the people here are fed, I hope someone is being heard. 749.title: Sabha: Indraprastha
749.hook: Yudhishthira asks Narada if he's ever seen a hall like this, and Narada describes the halls of the gods
749.carry: here is what the sky looks like
749.howItsDone: In Hindu tradition, Indra, Yama, Varuna and Kubera are among the guardians of the directions, the lokapalas, and their images can be found at the cardinal points of some temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Narada in the sabha, asking about soldiers, farmers and widows. Your line was each question opening with I hope.

It's a very human question. The questions are over, the king has promised to do better, and then Yudhishthira asks Narada something else. You've traveled through every world, he says. Have you ever seen a hall like this one, or a better one? He's sitting in the hall Maya built; of course he wants to know. And Narada's answer is careful. Among humans, he says, never. But there are other halls.
screen: `HAVE YOU SEEN A HALL LIKE THIS?` → `AMONG HUMANS, NEVER.` → `BUT THERE ARE OTHER HALLS.`

segments.voice: Then Narada describes them, one after another, the halls of the gods. The hall of Indra, king of the gods. Of Yama, lord of the dead. Of Varuna, out among the waters. Of Kubera, lord of wealth. And the hall of Brahma, the creator, which Narada says can't be properly described at all, because its form keeps changing. Listen to how he describes them. He tells what they're made of and how bright they are, but mostly he lists who sits there. Sages. Kings of old. Ancestors. Rivers and mountains, in person. Each hall is known by its gathering: the word sabha again, a room and the assembly in it. Narada's whole answer is a tour of assemblies. And look at what it does. Yudhishthira asked a proud question, maybe a fair one: is mine the best? Narada doesn't say no, and doesn't flatter. He opens the frame wider. Nothing among humans matches your hall. Here is what the sky looks like. A gentle way to take someone down a step without shaming them at all. It's also a setup. In Yama's hall, among the kings who've died, is someone Yudhishthira would know. Tomorrow, he'll ask. This week ran from Arjuna at the bow to the halls of the gods. The serial keeps doing this: a bright scene, then a wider one around it.
screen: `INDRA, YAMA, VARUNA, KUBERA.` · `BRAHMA'S HALL KEEPS CHANGING.` · `EACH HALL KNOWN BY WHO SITS THERE.` · `THE FRAME OPENS WIDER.` · then, large: `NOTHING LIKE IT ON EARTH. HERE IS THE SKY.`
